terms: Remembering a function's result so that when the same input comes again, it doesn't have to be calculated again.
The place where old answers are kept.
Same input → always the same output, and nothing else in the world changes.
js-mastery/memoization.what:
If a function is heavy and the same input keeps coming, calculating it every time is a waste.

Keep the answer in a cache (usually a Map). The next time the same input comes, give it straight from there.
js-mastery/memoization.analogy: Typing 17 × 23 into the calculator again and again. Work it out once and write it in a diary — next time look in the diary, don't punch it in again.
js-mastery/memoization.why: This works only when the function is pure — that is, the same input always gives the same output. If a function can give a different answer each time (like an API call or random), handing back the old answer would be wrong.
where: Fibonacci, DP problems — goes from exponential to linear.
useMemo and React.memo are the same idea — don't render again.
Writing memoize(fn) is often asked in machine coding.
pros: A huge speed benefit on repeated calculation.
Turns recursion from exponential to linear.
You don't have to change the function's code — just wrap it.
cons: Uses memory — the cache keeps growing.
Building a key for object arguments is hard and slow.
gotchas: Building the key with JSON.stringify depends on object key order and is slow on big data.
If the cache is never cleared it becomes a memory leak — use a size limit or a WeakMap.
Memoizing an impure function (API call, Date.now(), random) is a bug, not an optimization.

oop/o3_1.name: Getters and setters — let them read, don't let them change
oop/o3_1.desc: You want to show data outside but not let it be changed. And a setter is often the wrong answer.
terms: A method that reads the data and hands it over, but doesn't let it be changed.
A method that changes the data — and can check the rules while changing it.
A value that isn't stored but worked out every time — like "how many spots are free".
oop/o3_1.what:
You made #earnings private — but now whoever builds the report needs it. So what do we do?

Make a getter: a method that reads and hands over the value but doesn't let it be changed.

In TypeScript there are two ways: a normal method (getEarnings()) or the get keyword (get earnings()). The second one you read like a property — lot.earnings — but it is really a method.
oop/o3_1.why:
Now an important point, which many OOP tutorials teach wrongly.

Making a getter and setter for every private field defeats the whole point.

If you made #earnings private and then also made setEarnings(), you saved nothing — anyone can write lot.setEarnings(-99999). You just built a longer road to make the same mistake.

The right question is: "what does the outside need to do with this data?" Needs to build a report? Then give only a getter. Needs to collect a fee? Then give collectFee(amount) — which will check the rules inside.

How to do it:

A good rule:

• Getter — when the outside needs to see the value. Often right.
• Setter — when the outside needs to set the value directly. Often wrong. Give a task-oriented method instead (collectFee, park) that checks the rules inside itself.

And one small but lovely thing: some values shouldn't be stored at all. If you store "how many spots are free" it can go stale. Work it out every time instead. Such a value is called a derived value, and it can never be wrong.
gotchas: Making getter+setter for every field = the whole point of private is gone. This is the most common OOP mistake.
A getter for an array or object hands over the inside thing directly — and the outside can change it. Give a copy ([...arr]) or make it readonly.
get earnings() and #earnings can't have the same name without the #. That's why people write _earnings in TypeScript — but # is better.
Don't do heavy work inside a getter. People think it's a property (cheap), and read it 1000 times in a loop.

oop/o4_0.name: What is abstraction — and how it differs from encapsulation
oop/o4_0.desc: One hides data, the other hides the method. The two go together.
terms: Hiding the inner mess and showing the outside only what is necessary.
The actual code of "how it happens".
A promise — "I can do this job", without saying how.
oop/o4_0.what:
Think you drive a car. You turn the steering and the car turns. You don't need to know whether inside it's rack-and-pinion or hydraulic.

The steering wheel is an abstraction: it tells you what can be done (turning), and hides how it happens.

And the best part: if the company changes the steering's inner mechanism, you don't have to learn to drive again. That is the whole reward of abstraction.

Definition: Abstraction means exposing what an object can do while hiding how it does it.
oop/o4_0.why:
The easiest way to remember the difference:

Encapsulation — "don't touch my safe." (data)
Abstraction — "you don't need to know which company made the safe or how its lock works." (the method)

The two go together. Encapsulation makes abstraction possible: if the data isn't private, your "method" won't stay hidden, because people will touch the data directly and build their own method.

How to do it:

In our parking lot there are right now two places that need abstraction:

1. Payment. ParkingLot should only know: "money can be taken". Cash, UPI, card — that shouldn't be its headache.

2. Vehicle. Every vehicle has its own size and its own rate. ParkingLot should ask "what's your rate", not decide itself with an if-else.

Both need separate tools — and the next two lessons are exactly that.
gotchas: Abstraction doesn't mean "hide everything". Hide more than needed and people will look for workarounds. Hide only what can change.
In an interview you must be able to tell encapsulation and abstraction apart. Remember one line: encapsulation hides data, abstraction hides the method.

oop/o7_0.name: The mountain of subclasses — count it yourself
oop/o7_0.desc: Two different things together need four classes. Three things — eight.
terms: When two or three things combine and multiply the number of classes many times over.
Two things that are completely independent of each other — like "being electric" and "being handicap-accessible".
oop/o7_0.what:
You have Car, Bike, Truck. Now three new things arrive:

• Is it electric or not
• Is it for handicap use or not
• Is it VIP or not

These three are completely independent of each other — an electric vehicle can be handicap and VIP too. Such independent things are called orthogonal.

Now count: 3 vehicle types × 2 (electric or not) × 2 (handicap or not) × 2 (VIP or not) = 24 classes.
oop/o7_0.why:
And this isn't just a counting problem. Every new thing doubles the classes:

Add one more thing (like "is it diesel") → 48 classes.
One more → 96.

And most of these classes will have the same code copied. ElectricCar and ElectricTruck will both have the same plugIn() code written — because their parents are different and they can't share that code.

This is inheritance's biggest limit: it works in only one dimension.

How to do it:

The root of it is this: a class has only one parent (the rule from Chapter 5). So if you need two independent things together, the hierarchy has no room for them — you'll have to make a new class for every combination.

And when you build this mountain yourself and count it, you'll realise on your own what the answer should be: instead of making these things "classes", make them "things" that can be kept inside the vehicle.

But don't think about the answer yet. Today just build the mountain and count it.
gotchas: Really write this code, don't just read it. After writing eight classes the tiredness itself will tell you something is wrong — and that is the lesson of this chapter.
Don't think "I won't make so many classes". These classes get made one by one, over months, and each one feels right at the time.
In real codebases this mountain stands up by itself in 3 years. Nobody sits down one day and makes 24 classes.

oop/o12_0.name: Anti-patterns — the ones that got names
oop/o12_0.desc: God object, anemic model, and the mistakes you made yourself.
terms: A solution that looks fine at first but becomes a problem later.
One class that knows everything and does everything.
Classes that hold only data and no behaviour — procedural code in the mask of classes.
A method that uses another class's data more than its own class's.
Keeping everything as a number/string, even though it has its own rules.
oop/o12_0.what:
An anti-pattern means a solution that looks fine at first and becomes a burden later. The five most common:

1. God object — one class that does everything. Your ParkingLot from Chapter 9 was on this road: park, unpark, fee, SMS, report, CSV.

2. Anemic domain model — classes with only data, all the logic in separate "Service" classes. This comes from taking SRP too far.

3. Feature envy — a method that plays with other people's data more than its own.

4. Primitive obsession — the state before the Money in Chapter 9.

5. Shotgun surgery — one small change, five files (the if-else from Chapter 6).
oop/o12_0.why:
Pause a bit on the anemic domain model, because it is the most hidden one.

Many codebases look like this: class Ticket { id; plate; enteredAt; } — only data. And then class TicketService { calculateHours(t); isExpired(t); } — all the logic.

It works. But it is procedural code, just wearing a mask of classes. Data in one place, the functions that work on it in another — exactly the problem from Chapter 1, and the same harm: any Service can change Ticket's data.

And an honest point: in big systems this is sometimes chosen on purpose (when data comes from a DB and logic lives in separate layers). So don't blindly call it "bad" — just know what you are choosing.

How to do it:

Three measures to spot a god object:

1. The file is 300+ lines
2. The class has 10+ public methods
3. A one-line job can't be written without 2+ "and"s

And the test for feature envy: if a method touches some other object more than this, that method is in the wrong class. Pick it up and move it to where its data is.
gotchas: Don't blindly call an anemic domain model "bad". In big systems it is sometimes chosen on purpose (when data comes from a DB and validation is in a separate layer). Just know what you are choosing.
A god object isn't made in a day. Every method feels right at the time. So keep running the "and" test every 2-3 months.
The refactor for feature envy is the cheapest and has the biggest effect — pick the method up and put it in the class whose data it is using.

terms: A maximum limit on a metric or size that makes the build fail.
performance/t4_0.what: Definition: Budget = a limit: 'main JS ≤ 170KB gz', 'LCP ≤ 2.5s', 'CLS ≤ 0.1'. It is checked in CI; when a budget is broken the PR fails or warns.
performance/t4_0.why: Performance degrades slowly (a little more JS in every PR). A budget stops regressions before they merge, and gives the team a shared target.
cons: Very tight budgets can slow the team down
gotchas: Keep realistic (data-based) budgets, not aspirational ones
Lab metrics are noisy — take the median of multiple runs
Review budgets over time

terms: Cumulative Layout Shift — the page jumping around
Largest Contentful Paint — when the biggest content appeared
Flash of Unstyled Text — the default font showing before the font loads
react-mastery/nextjs-optimisations.what:
Definition: Next.js's built-in optimizers:

  • next/image — automatic resize, WebP/AVIF, lazy load, blur placeholder
  • next/font — fonts self-hosted at build time, zero layout shift
  • metadata export — SEO tags on the server
  • next/script — control over loading of third-party scripts
react-mastery/nextjs-optimisations.why: These three directly affect Core Web Vitals (which count in Google ranking). An image without width/height gives CLS; if Google Fonts come from the CDN there's an extra DNS + connection + FOUT; if metadata is set on the client the crawler doesn't see it at all.
where: next/font — never use the Google Fonts link
pros: Core Web Vitals get better automatically
Fonts are self-hosted — no external request
Images are converted to WebP/AVIF automatically
cons: External images need a domain whitelist
Outside Vercel, image optimization has its own cost
gotchas: Put priority on an above-the-fold image — otherwise it will lazy load and hurt LCP
When using fill, position:relative on the parent and the sizes prop are essential
Don't bring Google Fonts with <link> — bring them with next/font, otherwise FOUT and an extra request

real-world-scenarios/works-locally.q: How would you solve this problem? Works locally, broken in production
real-world-scenarios/works-locally.what:
“A feature you built works perfectly in local dev but misbehaves in production. What are the likely causes and how do you debug it?”

Concepts: Prod builds · Env vars at build time · CORS · SameSite cookies · CDN caching · Staging parity

What is being tested: Do you understand dev vs prod differences, not just your framework.

real-world-scenarios/fe-300-requests.q: How would you solve this problem? Search input fires 300+ requests with no debounce
real-world-scenarios/fe-300-requests.what:
"Users type in a search box and the network tab shows hundreds of requests being fired — one per keystroke. The server is getting hammered. You see 300+ requests for a single search query. Design the fix."

Concepts: Debounce · AbortController · Request cancellation · React Query deduplication · Minimum query length · Search-as-you-type patterns

What is being tested: Debounce/throttle patterns, AbortController, request cancellation, and the search UX best practices.

real-world-scenarios/deploy-broke-prod.q: How would you solve this problem? Your deploy just broke production
real-world-scenarios/deploy-broke-prod.what:
“You deployed at 3 PM. At 3:05 error rates are 10x. It's your change. Walk me through the next 15 minutes, and how you'd make deploys safer long-term.”

Concepts: Rollback first · Incident comms · Expand/contract migrations · Canary rollout · Feature flags · Blameless postmortem

What is being tested: Incident ownership, rollback-first instinct, blameless prevention thinking.

ai-system-design/sd7_5.why:
A prompt edited in a dashboard is an unreviewed production deploy with no rollback. A one-word change can move quality several percent and nobody will know which word.

How to do it:

Prompts in the repo, eval gate on the pull request, prompt version stamped into every trace.

build-mini-react/l4_2.why:
What you get: the comfort of JSX; a single network request; a smaller bundle through minify + tree-shaking; HMR, which reloads code while keeping state; imports from node_modules (without writing a URL); TypeScript, CSS modules, images — everything.

What you give up: your code and the browser's code are now different — you need source maps for debugging; one more config file that will break; 200MB in node_modules; build time; and the biggest thing — one more thing you'll have to understand.

How to do it:

This decision isn't mechanical, it's situational. A small learning project, one or two files, for learning → zero tooling is better, because you see exactly what is running. A big app, a team, TypeScript, 50+ files → the cost of tooling is paid back.

This question comes up in interviews. The right answer isn't "use Vite" — the right answer is "what is this giving me in exchange for what, and which matters more in my case".

build-mini-react/l11_2.why:
Once you have resumable work, a lot becomes possible:

• If more important work comes in the middle, do it first (priority)
• Throw the work away if it has gone stale (the user typed more)
• Hold a piece of work back until the data arrives (Suspense)

We won't build any of these — but now you can say how they are possible. And that is exactly what gets asked in interviews.

How to do it:

One small but important detail: we keep a wipRoot (work in progress root) and a currentRoot (what is on the screen right now). Work happens on wipRoot, the screen shows currentRoot.

Having these two separate trees is the foundation of Phase 12. And it's a well-known pattern — in graphics it is called double buffering: write to one buffer, show the other, then swap.

cons: Rare at runtime and hard to reproduce
Error handling and cancellation are subtle
A sequential await accidentally becomes serial
It is viewport-based, not component-based (container queries are the answer to this)

css-mastery/viewport-units.what:
Definition: vw/vh are viewport-relative. On mobile the address bar hides and shows on scroll, so 100vh assumes a fixed (large) viewport and content can hide under the bar.

Fix: dvh (dynamic, changes with the bar), svh (always safe, small), lvh (with the bar removed).

css-mastery/reflow-repaint.why: The fewer stages are triggered, the cheaper it is. That's why animations are done with transform/opacity and the DOM isn't read/written again and again.

css-mastery/layout-thrash.why: In a loop over 100 elements, 100 layouts happen; if you batch the reads, only 1. This is the most common cause of 'animation/measuring with JS causes jank'.

css-mastery/web-vitals.why: These are also Google search ranking signals and are directly tied to conversion. Lab data (Lighthouse) and field data (CrUX) can differ; real users' data is the field data.

database/sql10.what:
A Recursive CTE (WITH RECURSIVE) is a query that refers to itself — perfect for hierarchical data (org chart, category tree, graph). It has two members:

1) Anchor — the starting rows (like the top manager). 2) Recursive member — joins the anchor's results with the CTE to get the next level. This continues until no new row is produced (termination). If there's no de-duplication on each round, is the loop infinite? Careful: cycles can sneak in — keep a visited/level column.

oop/o9_2.desc: A Money class that simply cannot be negative. And the trap of readonly.

oop/o10_3.desc: These are not separate rules. They are five faces of one thing.

dsa/big-o.why:
The interviewer asks "what's the complexity?" because that one question tells whether you wrote the code or thought about it. Someone who can't state the cost of their own solution can't improve it either.

And in real work: that O(n²) loop takes 200ms on staging (100 rows), 30 seconds on prod (50,000 rows). Same code, different data — and you only find out when the customer screams.

How to think:

1. Identify n — the part of the input that can get big: array length, string size, tree nodes.
2. Count the loops and recursive calls. A loop inside a loop = multiply (n × n). One loop after another = add (n + n).
3. In a sum, keep only the biggest term — n² + n + 50 becomes n². Because at n = 10,000, n² is 10 crore and n is just 10 thousand — the small term vanishes.
4. Throw away constants — 3n → O(n).
5. Count space separately: extra arrays + recursion depth. 90% of people forget this step.

dsa/dfs.analogy:
Boxes inside a cupboard, and boxes inside those boxes. You open one box, go in completely through its first sub-box, and only then come back to open the next.
When you jot a note — as soon as you open the box, in the middle, or while closing it — those are the three orders. The route stays exactly the same.

dsa/dp-state-machine.what:
You're given a stock's price each day. Buy, sell, or do nothing — what's the maximum profit?

If you write only dp[i] = “max profit up to day i” here, you'll get stuck. Because the next decision depends on one more thing that isn't in this number: do you hold a stock right now or not?

If you hold a stock you can sell today. If you don't, you can buy. The options themselves are different.

So put that fact into the state. dp[i][0] = the best when you don't hold a stock, dp[i][1] = the best when you do. Now on each day each state has just two roads — stay where you are, or switch to the other state (by buying or selling).

That's the pattern. And it scales too — add a third state for a cooldown, add one more dimension for k transactions.

dsa/greedy.what:
Greedy means: at each step take the choice that looks best right now, and never look back. No table, no recursion — the job is done in one pass.

When it works it's the cleanest and fastest solution. There's only one problem: it often doesn't work, and when it doesn't, no error appears — the answer is simply wrong.

So the real work of greedy isn't writing code, it's deciding whether greedy will work.

There are two ways. Exchange argument: suppose the optimal answer did something else at the first step — now swap it for the greedy choice. If the answer never gets worse, greedy is right. Or a counterexample: find one small input where greedy fails. Found it? Then greedy won't work — reach for DP.

frontend-system-design/t2-1.what:
Definition: 10,000 rows of DOM kill the browser. In virtualization only ~20 visible rows get DOM; the scrollbar's height is faked with a spacer.

In a design round this is the standard answer for a "large list" — but saying it alone isn't enough, you have to state its tradeoffs.

frontend-system-design/t2-4.why:
An empty state should have two forms because the user's need differs. "No orders yet" → they need a button to start shopping. "This filter found nothing" → they need a button to clear the filter. Showing a single "No data" is useless in both cases.

And a skeleton is better than a spinner because it reserves the layout — the page doesn't jump when the content arrives (CLS = 0).

js-mastery/prototype-chain.what:
In JS every object has a hidden link — to its prototype. When you ask for obj.foo and it isn't on the object, JS follows that link. Not found there either, then further up. Until null.

This chain is called the prototype chain. This is JS's inheritance.

js-mastery/mixins.what:
In JS a class can have only one parent. But often you need behaviour from two or three places.

A mixin is the workaround: keep the behaviour in a plain object or function, and mix it in to whoever needs it.

nodejs-internals/njs-v8.why: This explains why JS is fast (JIT), why GC, and why Node perf tuning looks at V8 flags. It is the first step of an interview deep dive — keeping the V8 vs Node boundary clear.

nodejs-internals/nmo3.analogy: Two friends sharing work (A and B). B asks A to "bring the dairy" while A has done only half the job — A hands over only what has been made so far (partial). If you need the full thing, call a function (lazy), which resolves later.
nodejs-internals/nmo3.what:
Node caches modules by the resolved filename. That's why require('./a') twice → the same object (a singleton), and the code ran only once.

Circular dependency (A→B→A): when B requires A, A may still be incomplete — Node returns the partially-built module.exports (whatever has been set so far). That means in a circular case you will not get a property that was added to A after B's require.
nodejs-internals/nmo3.why: Circular deps happen in big codebases — partial exports cause silent undefined bugs. Knowing this = a common senior interview topic. Cache also means singleton — state sharing.

os-fundamentals/fcfs-sjf.what:
FCFS — the simplest. Whichever process arrived first at the market gets the CPU. Order = arrival order. The problem: if one long process comes, everyone behind it waits — the convoy effect (a traffic jam).

SJF — shortest job first. This makes the average wait time optimal. But the problem: you don't know the future (which one will be how long), and if short ones keep arriving, the big one starves to death.

SRTF — the preemptive version of SJF: whenever a new shorter one arrives, stop the running process and give it the CPU.

os-fundamentals/message-queues.why: When processes have to talk in structured data and you don't want the hassle of managing it yourself — a message queue is ideal. When it's request-response or a network — sockets. This is the practical toolkit of IPC choices: speed (shared) vs convenience (message) vs flexibility (socket).

react-mastery/first-component.what:
Definition: A React component is a normal JavaScript function that returns JSX. There is only one rule — the name must start with a capital letter.

function Button() = component. function button() = React will treat it as an HTML tag and break.

react-mastery/useeffect.why:
Cleanup running every time is exactly what saves you from a race condition. You change the user quickly — 3 fetches start. Without cleanup, whichever arrives latest wins, even if it is for the old user. With an abort in cleanup, only the latest request survives.

React 18's guidance: useEffect is not ideal for data fetching. Use React Query or a framework loader — they handle caching, dedup, retry, everything.

react-mastery/useref.what:
Definition: useRef(init) gives an object { current: init } that stays the same object for the component's entire life. Changing .current does not cause a re-render.

Two jobs: (1) grabbing a DOM node, (2) holding a value that must be remembered but has nothing to do with the UI (timer id, previous value, flag).

react-mastery/rerender-causes.why: The biggest misconception: "props changed, that's why it rendered". The truth is the opposite — the child rendered because the parent rendered, even if the props are exactly the same. Understanding this shows the right path to optimization: before memoizing props, stopping the parent's render or pushing state down is more effective.

react-mastery/usedeferredvalue.what:
Definition: const deferred = useDeferredValue(value) gives a "lagging" version of the value. React first updates the urgent UI with the new value, then renders again in the background with the deferred value.

The difference from useTransition: in a transition you wrap the update (you need control over the source); in a deferred value you wrap the value — it works even when the source belongs to someone else (props, a library's hook).

real-world-scenarios/be-graceful-shutdow.what:
“Every deploy causes a spike of 502 errors lasting about 10 seconds. Users see blank pages or failed API calls. The health checks pass quickly and the new pods are ready. Why are requests being dropped during the transition?”

Concepts: Graceful shutdown · Connection draining · SIGTERM handler · PreStop hooks · Load balancer deregistration · TerminationGracePeriodSeconds

What is being tested: Graceful shutdown, connection draining, and the gap between "pod ready" and "old pod fully drained".

typescript-mastery/assertion-fns.what: A type guard returns true/false and you write an if. An assertion function throws when it's wrong — and after that line TypeScript accepts the type as correct. No if.

typescript-mastery/component-typing.what:
A React component is a normal function that takes an object. So typing it is just like typing a normal function — no special React magic.

You don't even need to write the return type — TypeScript works it out from the JSX itself.

typescript-mastery/type-safe-builder.what:
The fluent form of the builder pattern — db.from("users").where(...).select(...).

And with type tracking the return type changes at each step, so autocomplete shows only the next valid step.
